title: Part 3, Chapter 6
paragraphs: "I don't believe it! I can't believe it!" Razumihin kept repeating, trying in bewilderment to refute Raskolnikov's arguments.

They were by now approaching Bakaleyev's lodgings, where Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia had been expecting them for some time. Razumihin kept stopping along the way in the heat of discussion, confused and excited by the very fact that for the first time they were speaking openly about it.
"Then don't believe it," Raskolnikov answered with a cold, careless smile. "As usual, you noticed nothing, but I was weighing every word."

"You're suspicious. That's why you weighed their words. Hmm, certainly, I agree Porfiry's tone was rather odd, and especially that wretch Zametov! You're right, there was something about him—but why? Why?"
"He's changed his mind since last night."
"Quite the contrary! If they had that brainless idea, they'd do their utmost to hide it and conceal their cards, so as to catch you later. But that was all so brazen and careless."

"If they had facts—real facts—or at least some grounds for suspicion, then of course they'd try to hide their game, hoping to get more. They would have searched my room long ago. But they have no facts—not one. It's all a mirage, all ambiguous. A floating idea, nothing more. So they try to throw me off with sheer brazenness. And maybe he was just irritated at having no facts and blurted things out in his annoyance. Or maybe he has a plan. He seems like an intelligent man. Perhaps he wanted to frighten me by letting on that he knows. That's their kind of psychology, brother. But it's sickening to explain it all. Stop!"

"And it's insulting, insulting! I understand you. But since we've started speaking openly now—and it's an excellent thing we have, I'm glad—I'll admit frankly that I've noticed this from them for a while. The merest hint, of course, just an insinuation—but why even an insinuation? How dare they? What possible basis? If you only knew how furious I've been! Think about it: simply because a poor student, unhinged by poverty and depression, on the eve of a severe illness with delirium—note that—suspicious, proud, vain, who hasn't spoken to a soul in six months, dressed in rags and boots with holes in them, has to stand before some wretched policemen and endure their insolence. An unexpected debt shoved in his face, an I.O.U. from Chebarov, fresh paint, thirty degrees of heat, a stifling room, a crowd of people, talk about the murder of someone he'd just visited—and all on an empty stomach! Anyone might faint! And that's what they base everything on! Damn them! I understand how maddening it is, but in your place, Rodya, I'd laugh at them—or better yet, spit in their ugly faces, a dozen times in every direction. I'd lash out neatly and put an end to it. Damn them! Chin up!"
"Still, he put it well," Raskolnikov thought.

"Damn them? But there's another interrogation tomorrow!" he said bitterly. "Do I really have to go explaining myself to them? I'm already disgusted that I lowered myself to talk to Zametov at the restaurant yesterday."
"Damn it! I'll go to Porfiry myself. I'll squeeze it out of him as a relative. He has to tell me the whole story. As for Zametov—"
"He's finally seeing through it," thought Raskolnikov.

"Wait!" cried Razumihin, seizing him by the shoulder. "Wait! You're wrong. I've thought it through. You're wrong! How was that a trap? You say the question about the workmen was a trap. But think: if you had done that, would you have admitted to seeing the painters at the apartment? On the contrary—you'd have seen nothing, even if you had. Who would volunteer evidence against himself?"
"If I had done that thing, I would certainly have said I'd seen the workmen and the apartment," Raskolnikov answered with reluctance and obvious distaste.
"But why speak against yourself?"

"Because only peasants and the greenest novices deny everything flatly under questioning. Any man with the slightest development and experience will certainly try to acknowledge all the external facts that can't be avoided, while seeking other explanations for them—introducing some special, unexpected twist that gives them a different meaning and puts them in a different light. Porfiry could very well have expected me to answer that way—to say I'd seen them, for the sake of plausibility, and then offer some explanation."

"But he would have told you immediately that the workmen couldn't have been there two days before, and that therefore you must have been there on the day of the murder, at eight o'clock. And he'd have caught you on a detail."

"Yes, exactly—he was counting on that. He was counting on me not having time to think it through, and rushing to give the most plausible answer, forgetting that the workmen couldn't have been there two days earlier."
"But how could you forget that?"

"Nothing easier. It's precisely on such simple things that clever people are most easily caught. The more cunning a man is, the less he suspects he'll be tripped up by something obvious. The more cunning the man, the simpler the trap must be. Porfiry is not the fool you think."
"He's a scoundrel, then, if that's the case!"

Raskolnikov couldn't help laughing. But at the same moment he was struck by the strangeness of his own candor and the eagerness with which he'd made this explanation, given that he'd maintained the entire preceding conversation with grim reluctance, obviously with a purpose, out of necessity.

"I'm developing a taste for certain aspects of this," he thought. But almost instantly he became uneasy, as though a sudden and alarming idea had occurred to him. His anxiety kept growing. They had just reached the entrance to Bakaleyev's.
"Go in alone!" Raskolnikov said suddenly. "I'll be right back."
"Where are you going? We're already here!"
"I have to. I'll come in half an hour. Tell them."
"Whatever you say—I'll come with you."

"You want to torture me too!" he screamed, with such bitter irritation, such despair in his eyes, that Razumihin dropped his hands. He stood on the steps for some time, watching gloomily as Raskolnikov strode rapidly away toward his lodging. Finally, gritting his teeth and clenching his fists, he swore to himself he'd squeeze Porfiry like a lemon that very day, and went upstairs to reassure Pulcheria Alexandrovna, who was by now alarmed by their long absence.

When Raskolnikov got home, his hair was soaked with sweat and he was breathing hard. He hurried up the stairs, walked into his unlocked room, and immediately bolted the door. Then, in senseless terror, he rushed to the corner—to the hole in the wallpaper where he had hidden the things. He put his hand in and for several minutes carefully felt through every crack and fold of the paper. Finding nothing, he stood up and drew a deep breath. Walking up to Bakaleyev's steps, he had suddenly imagined that something—a chain, a stud, or even a bit of the wrapping paper with the old woman's handwriting on it—might somehow have slipped out and been lost in some crack, only to turn up later as unexpected, conclusive evidence against him.

He stood as though lost in thought, and a strange, humiliated, half-senseless smile played on his lips. He picked up his cap and quietly left the room. His thoughts were all tangled. He walked dreamily through the gateway.
"Here he is himself!" a loud voice shouted.
He raised his head.

The porter stood at the door of his little room, pointing him out to a short man who looked like a workman—wearing a long coat and a waistcoat and, from a distance, remarkably resembling a woman. He was stooped, and his head in a greasy cap hung forward. From his wrinkled, flabby face, he looked over fifty; his small eyes, buried in fat, stared out grimly, sternly, and with displeasure.
"What is it?" Raskolnikov asked, going up to the porter.
The man stole a look at him from under his brows, studied him attentively and deliberately, then slowly turned and walked out through the gate into the street without a word.
"What was that about?" Raskolnikov cried.
"That fellow was asking if a student lived here—mentioned your name and who you lodge with. Then I saw you coming and pointed you out, and he left. Strange."
The porter seemed somewhat puzzled, but not very. After wondering for a moment, he turned and went back to his room.

Raskolnikov ran after the stranger and immediately spotted him walking along the other side of the street with the same even, deliberate step, eyes fixed on the ground, as though deep in thought. He quickly caught up but walked behind him for some time. At last he drew level and looked at the man's face. The man noticed him at once, glanced at him quickly, then lowered his eyes again. They walked side by side for a minute without saying a word.
"You were asking for me at the porter's?" Raskolnikov said at last, in a strangely quiet voice.
The man gave no answer. He didn't even look at him. Again they walked in silence.
"Why do you come and ask for me and then say nothing? What's the meaning of it?"
Raskolnikov's voice broke; he seemed unable to articulate clearly.
The man raised his eyes and turned a dark, sinister look on Raskolnikov.
"Murderer!" he said suddenly, in a quiet but clear and distinct voice.

Raskolnikov walked on beside him. His legs suddenly went weak, a cold shiver ran down his spine, and his heart seemed to stop for a moment, then began pounding as though it had broken free. They walked like that for about a hundred paces, side by side, in silence.
The man did not look at him.
"What do you mean? What are you—who is a murderer?" Raskolnikov muttered, barely audible.
"You are a murderer," the man answered, still more distinctly and emphatically, with a smile of triumphant hatred, and again looked straight into Raskolnikov's pale face and stricken eyes.

They had reached an intersection. The man turned left without looking back. Raskolnikov stood rooted to the spot, staring after him. He watched the man turn around about fifty paces away and look back at him, still standing there. Raskolnikov couldn't see clearly, but he thought the man was smiling that same smile of cold hatred and triumph.

With slow, faltering steps, knees shaking, Raskolnikov made his way back to his little garret, chilled all over. He took off his cap, put it on the table, and for ten minutes stood without moving. Then he sank exhausted onto the sofa and, with a feeble moan of pain, stretched himself out. He lay there for half an hour.

He thought of nothing. Thoughts or fragments of thoughts, images without order or connection floated through his mind—faces of people he'd seen in childhood or met somewhere and would never have recalled, the bell tower of a church in V., a billiard table in a restaurant with officers playing, the smell of cigars in an underground tobacco shop, a tavern room, a dark back staircase soaked with dirty water and littered with eggshells, and Sunday bells drifting in from somewhere. The images followed one another, spinning like a hurricane. Some he liked and tried to hold onto, but they faded. There was a tightness inside him, but it wasn't crushing—at times it was even pleasant. The slight shivering persisted, but that too was an almost pleasant sensation.

He heard Razumihin's hurried footsteps and closed his eyes, pretending to be asleep. Razumihin opened the door and stood in the doorway for a while, as though hesitating, then stepped softly into the room and went cautiously to the sofa. Raskolnikov heard Nastasya whisper:
"Don't disturb him! Let him sleep. He can eat later."
"Right," Razumihin answered. They both withdrew carefully and closed the door. Another half hour passed. Raskolnikov opened his eyes, turned on his back, and clasped his hands behind his head.

"Who is he? Who is that man who sprang from the earth? Where was he, what did he see? He saw everything, that's clear. Where was he then, and from where did he see? Why has he only now sprung up? And how could he see? Is it possible?" Raskolnikov continued, going cold and shivering. "And the jewel case Nikolay found behind the door—was that possible? A clue? You miss an infinitesimal detail and you can build a whole pyramid of evidence on it! A fly buzzed past and saw it! Is it possible?" He felt with sudden loathing how weak, how physically weak he had become. "I should have known," he thought with a bitter smile. "And how dared I, knowing myself, knowing what I'd be like, take up an axe and shed blood! I should have known beforehand. But I did know!" he whispered in despair. At times he came to a standstill on some thought.

"No, those men aren't made that way. The real Master, to whom all is permitted, storms Toulon, massacres in Paris, forgets an army in Egypt, wastes half a million men in the Moscow campaign, and gets off with a joke at Vilna. And altars are built to him after his death. So all is permitted. No, such men are made not of flesh but of bronze!"

One sudden, irrelevant thought nearly made him laugh. Napoleon, the pyramids, Waterloo—and a miserable, scrawny old woman, a pawnbroker with a red trunk under her bed! A fine hash for Porfiry Petrovitch to digest! How could they? It's too inartistic. "A Napoleon crawling under an old woman's bed!" Ugh, how disgusting!

At moments he felt he was raving. He sank into feverish agitation. "The old woman is beside the point," he thought hotly and incoherently. "The old woman was perhaps a mistake, but she's not what matters! The old woman was only an illness. I was in a hurry to overstep the line. I didn't kill a human being—I killed a principle! I killed the principle, but I didn't overstep—I stopped on this side. All I proved was that I could only kill. And it seems I couldn't even do that. Principle? Why was that fool Razumihin railing against the socialists? They're industrious, commercial people—'the happiness of all' is their cause. No, I only have one life and I won't have another. I don't want to wait for 'the happiness of all.' I want to live myself, or else not live at all. I simply couldn't walk past my mother starving while clutching my rouble, waiting for 'universal happiness.' 'I'm adding my little brick to the happiness of all, and so my heart is at peace.' Ha-ha! Why did you let me slip through? I only live once; I too want— Ugh, I'm nothing but an aesthetic louse!" he added, suddenly laughing like a madman. "Yes, I am definitely a louse," he went on, clutching at the idea, gloating over it, savoring it with vindictive pleasure. "First, because I can reason that I am one; and second, because for a whole month I've been troubling benevolent Providence, calling it to witness that I wasn't acting for selfish pleasure but with a grand and noble purpose—ha-ha! Third, because I aimed at carrying it out as justly as possible, weighing and measuring and calculating. Of all the lice I chose the most useless and proposed to take from her only as much as I needed for the first step, nothing more—the rest would have gone to a monastery, according to her will—ha-ha! And what proves beyond doubt that I am utterly a louse," he added, grinding his teeth, "is that I'm perhaps viler and more loathsome than the louse I killed, and I knew beforehand that I'd tell myself this after killing her. Can anything compare with that horror? The vulgarity! The baseness! I understand the 'prophet' with his sabre on his steed: Allah commands, and trembling creation must obey! The 'prophet' is right—he's right when he plants a cannon across a street and mows down the innocent and guilty alike without deigning to explain! Submit, trembling creature, and don't you dare have desires—that's not for you! I shall never, never forgive the old woman!"
His hair was soaked with sweat; his trembling lips were parched; his eyes stared at the ceiling.

"Mother, sister—how I loved them! Why do I hate them now? Yes, I hate them. I feel a physical hatred for them. I can't bear them near me. I went to my mother and kissed her, I remember. To embrace her and think: if she only knew—should I tell her, then? That's just the sort of thing I might do. She must be like me," he added, straining to think through his delirium. "Oh, how I hate the old woman now! I think I'd kill her again if she came back to life! Poor Lizaveta! Why did she have to come in? It's strange, though—why do I almost never think about her, as if I hadn't killed her? Lizaveta! Sonia! Poor, gentle creatures with gentle eyes. Dear women! Why don't they weep? Why don't they moan? They give up everything. Their eyes are soft and gentle. Sonia, Sonia! Gentle Sonia!"

He lost consciousness. It seemed strange to him that he couldn't remember how he'd gotten into the street. It was late evening. Twilight had fallen and the full moon shone brighter and brighter, but there was a peculiar breathlessness in the air. The streets were crowded—workers and businessmen heading home, others out for a walk. There was a smell of plaster, dust, and stagnant water. Raskolnikov walked along, mournful and anxious. He was distinctly aware of having come out with a purpose, of needing to do something urgently, but he'd forgotten what. Suddenly he stopped and saw a man on the other side of the street, beckoning to him. He crossed over, but at once the man turned and walked away with his head hanging, as though he'd made no sign. "Wait—did he really beckon?" Raskolnikov wondered, but tried to catch up. When he was within ten paces, he recognized the man and was frightened: it was the same stooped man in the long coat. Raskolnikov followed at a distance; his heart was pounding. They turned down a side street; the man still didn't look back. "Does he know I'm following?" Raskolnikov thought. The man entered the gateway of a large house. Raskolnikov hurried to the gate and peered in. In the courtyard, the man turned and again seemed to beckon. Raskolnikov followed at once, but the man had vanished. He must have gone up the first staircase. Raskolnikov rushed after him. He could hear slow, measured footsteps two flights above. The staircase seemed strangely familiar. He reached the window on the first floor; the moon shone through the panes with a melancholy, mysterious light. Then the second floor. This was the apartment where the painters had been working! But how had he not recognized it at once? The footsteps above had died away. "He must have stopped or hidden somewhere." He reached the third floor. Should he go on? The silence was dreadful. But he went on. The sound of his own footsteps frightened him. How dark it was! The man must be hiding in some corner. Then he saw it—the apartment door was standing wide open. He hesitated and went in. The passage was very dark and empty, as though everything had been removed. He crept on tiptoe into the parlour, which was flooded with moonlight. Everything was as before: the chairs, the mirror, the yellow sofa, the pictures in their frames. A huge, round, copper-red moon looked in at the windows. "It's the moon that makes it so still, weaving some mystery," he thought. He stood and waited—waited a long time—and the more silent the moonlight, the harder his heart pounded, until it hurt. And still the same hush. Suddenly there was a momentary sharp crack, like a splinter snapping, and then all was still again. A fly buzzed up and struck the windowpane with a plaintive drone. At that moment he noticed, in the corner between the window and the small cupboard, something like a cloak hanging on the wall. "Why is that cloak here?" he thought. "It wasn't there before." He went up quietly and realized someone was hiding behind it. He carefully moved the cloak aside and saw, sitting in a chair in the corner, the old woman—bent double, her face hidden. He stood over her. "She's afraid," he thought. He stealthily took the axe from the loop and struck her once on the skull, then again. But strangely she didn't stir, as though made of wood. He was frightened. He bent closer, trying to see her face, but she bent her head even lower. He bent down to the ground and peered up at her face from below—and went cold with horror: the old woman was sitting there laughing, shaking with silent laughter, straining with all her might not to let him hear. Suddenly he thought he heard the bedroom door crack open, and there was laughter and whispering inside. Frenzy seized him. He began striking the old woman on the head with all his strength, but with every blow the laughter and whispering from the bedroom grew louder, and the old woman simply shook with mirth. He tried to run, but the passage was packed with people, the apartment doors stood open, and on the landing, on the stairs, everywhere below there were people—rows of heads, all watching, but huddled together in silence, waiting. Something gripped his heart; his legs wouldn't move; they were rooted to the spot. He tried to scream—and woke up.
He drew a deep breath—but his dream seemed strangely to persist: his door was flung open, and a man he had never seen stood in the doorway, watching him intently.
Raskolnikov had barely opened his eyes before he shut them again. He lay on his back, not moving.
"Is it still a dream?" he wondered, and again raised his eyelids the tiniest bit. The stranger was standing in the same place, still watching him.

He stepped carefully into the room, closed the door quietly behind him, went to the table, paused a moment—still keeping his eyes on Raskolnikov—and noiselessly sat down in the chair by the sofa. He placed his hat on the floor beside him and leaned on his cane, chin resting on his hands. It was clear he was prepared to wait indefinitely. As far as Raskolnikov could make out through stolen glances, the man was no longer young, stout, with a full, fair, nearly white beard.

Ten minutes passed. It was still light, but dusk was falling. The room was perfectly still. Not a sound came from the stairs. Only a large fly buzzed and fluttered against the windowpane. The silence became unbearable. Raskolnikov suddenly sat up on the sofa.
"Well, tell me what you want."
"I knew you weren't asleep but only pretending," the stranger answered, laughing calmly. "Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov—allow me to introduce myself."
